newsitem.title: INDIA: India may discuss weeds in wheat with Australia.
newsitem.headline: India may discuss weeds in wheat with Australia.

text.p: Indian Agriculture Ministry officials may visit Australia to discuss weeds in its wheat exports to India, government officials of both countries said on Friday.

"The Indian government's Agriculture Ministry officials will go later this year to Australia to discuss the issue of alleged contamination with exotic weeds," Australian high commissioner (ambassador) to India Darren Gribble told Reuters.
"The issue is going to be discussed with the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) and the Australian Plant Quarantine Inspection Service," Gribble said. He gave no other details.

Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra, who also holds the Food Ministry portfolio, said earlier this week that weeds were detected in wheat import shipments from Australia, but they were common in wheat of any origin and not harmful.
Analysts said the weed-infected wheat was not harmful if consumed, but would yield a smaller crop if used for sowing.
A senior Agriculture Ministry official said the government was considering sending a delegation to Australia to discuss the problem with the AWB but had not finalised its plans.
"We are still thinking," the official said. "Nothing has been finalised. If we go, talks will be held not only with the AWB, but also with the government."

India's state-run State Trading Corp (STC) has so far contracted to import 1.75 million tonnes, mainly from Australia, Argentina and Canada after India authorised the import of two million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97 (April-March) to build stocks and check rising prices.
The government announced the fresh import of two million tonnes of wheat in 1997/98, of which the STC has contracted for one million tonnes, mainly from Australia.
Officials said Australia, which has export contracts with India totalling 2.325 million tonnes, had so far shipped 1.3 million. The rest is due for shipment after July.
Gribble said Australia had abided by all requirements in its wheat sales to India.
"The issue is between the AWB and Indian buying agencies," Gribble added. "The matter has not been taken up at a government-to-government level."
On Thursday STC officials said India was unlikely to stop further wheat purchases from Australia, but might suggest new quality norms for future arrivals.

Reports from Australia earlier this week quoted AWB officials as saying Australia had abided by all requirements in its wheat sales to India and had not received any official complaints about quality.
